explanation: To a botanist, a berry is a fleshy fruit from a single ovary with the seeds inside. Strawberries swell from the flower's base, raspberries are clusters of tiny fruits, and cherries have a stone.

claims.text: In botanical terms, a banana is a berry.
In botanical terms, strawberries, raspberries and cherries are not berries.
A botanical berry is a fleshy fruit that develops from a single ovary and has its seeds inside the flesh.
The fleshy part of a strawberry develops from the receptacle at the base of the flower.
A raspberry is an aggregate fruit, a cluster of small drupelets.
A cherry is a drupe, with a stone around its seed.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: six listed. c1 is high because it is the key of a counterintuitive item, so C26 sets it high; the tooling's riskReason enum has no counterintuitive value yet (guide v1.1 adds one), so checker_doubt stands in for it; c2 states the other half of the same surprise, so I raised it to high too. One search on botanical berries should cover both. c3 to c6 are standard botany. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology, so none applies and every high-risk claim needs web evidence from checker A. rivalTest: the two '-berry' names are the planted trap. Argued against the key: cultivated bananas are seedless, but the fruit still forms as a berry from a single ovary, which is how botany classes it. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: all four fruits are sold worldwide; classified as Nature because it needs botany, not cooking. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 34 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a multiple-choice item. doubts: none on the botany. Food and Drink writers may use the same surprise, so the editor may see a cross-category near-duplicate.
